newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Thousands join Belgian steel workers in jobs march.
newsitem.headline: Thousands join Belgian steel workers in jobs march.

text.p: Thousands of demonstrators from across Belgium joined workers of bankrupt Belgian steel firm Forges de Clabecq SA Sunday in a peaceful protest against job losses, company closures and social injustice.

"The march is all about giving a voice back to the grass roots...asking them to take up their position again, and to insist on being heard," Roberto D'Orazio, leader of the socialist FGTB trade union at Clabecq, told Belgian radio.
Estimates of the number marching past Clabecq steel works near the town of Tubize, close to Brussels, varied between 35,000 and 50,000, Belgian media reported.
Clabecq trade unionists had called on everyone from factory workers and public sector employees to the unemployed, students, pensioners and children to join in.
Many arrived by coach or on special trains laid on by Belgian railways from several towns in the south of the country, carrying balloons and waving banners.
"What about me? Will I get a job?" read a placard held by one small boy wearing a steel worker's safety helmet. "Clabecq must live!" another banner proclaimed.

Among the crowd were some of the 2,000 workers at the privately-owned Boel steel plant in La Louviere, south-west of the capital, who face 800 job losses under a plan to merge Boel with Dutch steel firm Hoogovens.
Parents caught up in Belgium's pedophile and child murder scandal also came along to give their backing.

They led a "White March" in Brussels last October of 250,000 people who wanted to show their support for pedophile victims' families and to call for judicial reform. The parents said they were now concerned for the welfare of Clabecq workers' children.
"All these problems in Belgium are linked," said Gino Russo, a metalworker whose child was one of those killed in the affair.
Sunday's march built on the momentum of a rally in Brussels last week by 15,000 public sector workers worried about pensions and privatisation, and angry at plans to reform labour laws.

Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene's government has been cutting back on public spending and edging up taxes to ensure Belgium can meet the Maastricht criteria necessary to take part in a single European currency, planned for 1999.
He has also decided to impose a maximum 6.1 percent wage rise in 1997/1998, following a two-year wage freeze, after employers and workers failed to agree a deal themselves.

Belgium's latest jobless figures put unemployment at 13.6 percent in December. The figure is calculated differently from European Union rates, which showed Belgian unemployment at 9.5 percent in November -- the most recent month available.
Clabecq -- whose 1,800 workers now face an uncertain future -- was just one of 768 Belgian companies to go bankrupt in January, a record 36-percent leap from the same month in 1996.
Since Clabecq went bankrupt receivers have been trying to salvage the firm which has orders up to the end of March.
But Clabecq's majority shareholder and biggest creditor, Belgium's southern Walloon Region, last week turned down the receivers' request for 800 million francs worth of financing.
Meanwhile banks are appealing a court order requiring them to extend credit to Clabecq worth 650 million Belgian francs ($20.4 million).

Clabecq filed for bankruptcy in mid-December after the European Commission rejected a 1.5 billion Belgian franc ($47 million) rescue plan by the Walloon Region, which then withdrew its suppport for the firm.
